Single
SING-gul
a. (one only; not double or divided; free from duplicity; sincere and whole in intention)
Latin singulus, one at a time, one by one. English kept both the count — a single thing, not two — and the moral sense that grew from it, a single eye or a single heart being one undivided in its aim rather than split between two.

Biblical Definition

Christ's teaching on the eye, given in nearly identical words in Matthew and Luke, turns entirely on this second, moral sense of the word: The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light. The eye here stands for the whole inward aim of a man — what he is actually looking at, actually seeking, actually serving. A single eye is one fixed on one object without division; and Matthew's verse, read in its context between treasure laid up in heaven and the flat statement that no man can serve two masters, makes plain what the one object is meant to be.

The alternative Christ names is not merely distraction but an eye that is evil, and the whole body correspondingly full of darkness — the darkness of a man trying to serve God and mammon at once, whose inward light, precisely because it is divided, becomes no light at all. Singleness of eye, in this teaching, is not a a call to simplicity for its own sake; it is the necessary condition for a man's whole inward life to be illuminated by anything, because a light split between two objects has, by definition, stopped being a single light and become a confusion of shadows.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one only, not double; also, sincere; unmixed with deceit or hypocrisy; free from duplicity of intention.

expand to see more

SINGLE, a. One only; not double; also, sincere, honest, free from artifice or duplicity of aim.

EYE, n. The organ of sight; figuratively, the mind's power of perceiving, attending, and desiring.

LIGHT, n. That which makes objects visible; figuratively, knowledge, understanding, or spiritual illumination.

DARKNESS, n. Absence of light; figuratively, ignorance, sin, or spiritual blindness.

MAMMON, n. Riches; wealth personified as an object of worship rivaling the true God.

Key Scripture

Mat 6:22 — "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light."

Mat 6:23 — "But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!"

Mat 6:24 — "No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon."

Luk 11:34 — "The light of the body is the eye: therefore when thine eye is single, thy whole body also is full of light; but when thine eye is evil, thy body also is full of darkness."

Modern Corruption

Single-mindedness is praised as a mere personality trait, useful for productivity, when Christ ties it directly to the impossibility of serving two masters and warns that a divided eye fills the whole body with darkness.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself; single still means one and undivided. The principle worth recovering is the exact placement of Christ's saying, sandwiched between the command to lay up treasure in heaven rather than on earth and the flat statement that no man can serve two masters. The single eye is not a technique for a better life; it is the visible symptom of an undivided allegiance.

The warning cuts against every attempt to keep two ultimate loyalties running side by side, God and mammon, treasure on earth and treasure in heaven, hoping the eye can somehow serve both without going dark. Christ's language allows for no such balance: an eye that is not single is called evil, not merely inefficient, and the darkness it produces is total, filling the whole body, precisely because the light a man has was never meant to be divided in the first place.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek haplous (G573), single, simple, without folds; the word behind Christ's teaching on the eye in Matthew 6:22 and Luke 11:34.

expand to see more

Greek haplous (G573) — single, simple, sound, without folds or doubling; the adjective behind “single” in both Gospel accounts.

Greek haplotes (G572) — singleness, simplicity, sincerity; the noun form used elsewhere of a single-hearted generosity (2 Corinthians 8:2, Romans 12:8).

Greek poneros (G4190) — evil, bad, of poor quality; the word behind “evil” describing the divided eye.

Greek skotos (G4655) — darkness; the total condition of a body whose light has become divided.

Aramaic mamona (G3126) — mammon, riches personified; the second master a single eye cannot also serve.

Usage

"“if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light” — the promise of undivided sight."

"“if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness” — the warning that frames it."

"“Ye cannot serve God and mammon” — the divided allegiance a single eye refuses."
